title: Interpret and use information from texts

lessons.title: Reading work texts with purpose
lessons.html:
Texts a team leader must interpret

At NQF level 3 you are expected not only to find information in texts, but to interpret it: understand what it means, how it applies to your situation, and what action to take. In a packhouse, poultry plant or seed operation you will work with:

  • Standard operating procedures (SOPs) and work instructions
  • Export or customer specifications, such as size, colour and defect tolerances
  • Safety data sheets (SDS) and chemical labels
  • Audit reports and corrective action requests
  • Production reports, graphs and dashboards
  • Company policies, such as leave, disciplinary or HACCP policies
  • Memos, emails and notices from management

Reading strategies

  1. Preview: look at the title, headings, date, author and any summary. Ask what type of text it is and why it was written.
  2. Set a purpose: what do I need from this text?
  3. Skim for the overall message.
  4. Scan for specific details such as limits, dates or responsibilities.
  5. Read closely the sections that affect your work, more than once if needed.
  6. Summarise the main points in your own words.

Understanding vocabulary

Work texts contain technical terms such as 'tolerance', 'traceability', 'germination percentage', 'cold chain', 'non-conformance'. Use context clues, a glossary in the document, a dictionary or ask an expert. Keep a personal glossary of terms used in your workplace.

Understanding structure

Notice how a text is organised: numbered steps show sequence, tables show comparison, bullet lists show items of equal importance, and bold or boxed text shows warnings. Structure helps you find and understand information quickly.

lessons.title: Interpreting meaning: fact, opinion, bias and implication
lessons.html:
Reading critically

Not everything written is neutral fact. A team leader must judge what a text really says and how reliable it is.

Fact and opinion

  • Fact: can be checked. 'The pallet temperature on arrival was 9 °C.'
  • Opinion: a belief or judgement. 'The transport company is useless.'

Decisions should be based on facts. Opinions may be useful but need evidence.

Purpose and bias

Ask who wrote the text and why. A supplier's brochure aims to sell; it will emphasise benefits and may leave out disadvantages. A union newsletter and a management memo may describe the same wage negotiation differently. Look for loaded words, one-sided arguments or missing information.

Explicit and implied meaning

Some information is stated directly (explicit). Some is implied and must be inferred. If a memo says 'All overtime from next month must be approved in writing by the production manager', it implies that supervisors may no longer approve overtime themselves and that overtime is being watched more closely, possibly because of cost.

Interpreting instructions and rules

Read conditions carefully. Words like 'must', 'shall' and 'may not' signal compulsory rules. 'Should' signals strong recommendation; 'may' signals permission. 'Unless', 'except' and 'only if' change the meaning of a rule. Misreading these can lead to non-compliance.

Comparing texts

Sometimes two texts conflict, for example an old SOP and a new customer specification. Check dates and version numbers, identify which is current and approved, and ask your quality manager if unclear. Never choose the easier option without confirmation.

Visual texts

Graphs, charts and diagrams also need interpretation. Check the title, the axes and units, the scale and the time period. A graph with a scale that starts at 90% instead of 0% can make small changes look dramatic.

lessons.title: Using information to act and inform others
lessons.html:
From reading to action

The point of interpreting work texts is to act correctly and to help others understand.

Applying information

Example: a new export specification for citrus arrives. The team leader:

  1. Reads the specification and identifies what has changed, such as a new minimum size count and new label wording.
  2. Compares it with the current packing instruction.
  3. Lists actions: reset the sizer, update label templates, retrain packers, update the QC checklist.
  4. Confirms understanding with the quality manager.
  5. Briefs the team in simple language and checks their understanding.

Using a safety data sheet

An SDS has standard sections including identification, hazards, composition, first aid measures, fire-fighting, accidental release, handling and storage, exposure controls and PPE, and disposal. When introducing a new sanitiser, use the SDS to decide the PPE, storage conditions, first aid steps and spill response, and explain these to your team.

Summarising and reporting

Managers often ask team leaders to summarise long texts. A good summary:

  • States the source and date.
  • Gives the main points only, in your own words.
  • Highlights what affects your team and what action is needed.
  • Is short: often half a page or a few bullet points.

Passing information to others

Not all workers read easily or read English well. When you pass on information from texts, use plain language, demonstrate where possible, use pictures or samples, and translate key messages. Display updated notices clearly and remove outdated ones.

Document control

Use only current, approved versions of procedures and forms. Check version numbers and dates, and report outdated documents found in work areas.

Key points

  • Preview, set a purpose, skim, scan and then read closely.
  • Separate facts from opinions and watch for bias.
  • Read rule words like must, should, may and unless carefully.
  • Check dates and versions when texts conflict.
  • Turn information into clear actions and pass it on in plain language.
